acv.quote: A hundred and eighty K a year, on a three-year term.

header.tag_why: The deal moved from a bake-off to a win when a Fetchwell engineer used our docs and sandbox to build a working sitter payment flow over a weekend, and the decider was an engineering leader who said finance would sign what he brought them; the marketplace capabilities (sitter onboarding, identity checks, local-currency payouts for Canada and the UK) are the close second.

messaging_changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
messaging_changes.change: For marketplace and low-ticket prospects whose pain is operational rather than lost revenue, stop presenting the acceptance-rate slide in first calls. Spend that time on getting their providers paid locally and on freeing up their engineers. Keep M4 for buyers who raise authorization rates themselves.
messaging_changes.why: The rep presented the acceptance-rate slide in full and got 'Silence', and the decider dismissed it outright with 'our average booking is 38 dollars, I'm not losing sleep over auth rates.'

messaging_changes.current_line: Onboard, verify and pay out to sellers worldwide, in their local currency.
messaging_changes.change: For gig and service apps, use the buyer's words: 'Payments shouldn't be a team: get your sitters paid locally in every country you launch.' Swap 'sitters' for the prospect's own word for its providers. Say 'sitter pay', not 'payouts', and 'the app', not 'marketplace'. Only add a timing promise in the 'paid by Friday' style after we have confirmed we can meet it.
messaging_changes.why: The marketplace capabilities landed (E20), but the customer describes them as 'sitter pay' and 'paid by Friday' and wants payments not to be a team, while our line uses the category words they never say.

messaging_changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
messaging_changes.change: For engineering-led marketplace deals, open with the cost of running payments in-house instead of global growth: 'Stop babysitting your payments. Get your engineers back and ship the roadmap items payments keeps pushing.' Then present local-currency payouts as the way they launch new countries.
messaging_changes.why: Expansion was the occasion (E1), but the pain the customer described was two engineers 'more or less full-time just keeping sitter payments working', a faster-pay roadmap item 'pushed three quarters in a row', and wanting to 'stop babysitting this.'

messaging_changes.current_line: Built for developers: launch payments fast with our APIs, docs and sandbox.
messaging_changes.change: Keep the developer line, but end it with a call to action for the prospect's engineers: 'Build your own sitter pay flow in our sandbox before you decide.' Adapt 'sitter pay' to the prospect's use case. Make inviting that hands-on build a planned step in the sales motion, aimed at the engineering decider's team.
messaging_changes.why: The docs and sandbox landed, and the deal turned when an engineer built 'a working sitter payment flow over a weekend', after which 'Daniel stopped saying 'if''. The decider was engineering, but nothing in our motion invited or tracked that build.

gaps.insight: The 'clean one' was not clean. Three things were never resolved: the Venmo question, PayPal details pushed to implementation, and a saved-card migration reference that was promised and never delivered, which came back at kickoff as 'we'll find out.' The rep's claim that the customer chose to accept the risk is her own read, not something the customer said. What looks like a win could become an implementation failure on a three-year contract.
gaps.messaging: Build a clear PayPal/Venmo continuity answer and a saved-card migration customer story at comparable scale, so M8 'customer stories' covers the switching-risk question and not just logos.

language.insight: The customer's words are about relief and a promise to their sitters ('haunted house,' 'babysitting,' 'paid by Friday'). Ours are category words: marketplace, payouts, acceptance. The rep herself said 'marketplace piece' even though nobody at Fetchwell says marketplace, so our vocabulary is reaching the customer unfiltered.
language.messaging: Rewrite M11 in the buyer's terms, for example 'Payments shouldn't be a team: get sitter pay out by Friday in every country you launch,' and ban 'marketplace' and 'payouts' from first-call decks for gig and service apps.

gaps.follow_up: Ask Priya which provider Fetchwell is moving off, and whether the account-manager churn complaint was about the incumbent or Braintree.

close.rep_takeaway: A signature doesn't make a deal clean. Before you call it clean, list every 'I'll get back to you' and every question you danced around. Here, an unanswered Venmo question and an undelivered saved-card reference became a 'we'll find out' at kickoff on a three-year contract. Also, the engineer's weekend prototype won this deal and you only heard about it secondhand, so get close to the builders early and invite the sandbox test on purpose.
